paragraphs.modern: Aristophanes announced that he would take the discussion in a new direction: he meant to praise Love in a different way from either Pausanias or Eryximachus. 'Mankind,' he said, 'has never understood the power of Love at all, in my view — you can tell from the way people neglect him. If they had understood him, they would surely have built him noble temples and altars and offered solemn sacrifices in his honor. None of this is done, though it most certainly ought to be — for of all the gods, Love is the best friend of human beings: he is our helper, and the healer of the ills that are the greatest obstacle to the happiness of our race. I will try to explain his power to you, and you must pass on to the rest of the world what I am teaching you. First, let me explain human nature and what has happened to it, because our original nature was not the same as it is now, but different. Originally there were not two sexes, as there are now, but three: man, woman, and a union of the two. This third sex had a name to match its double nature. It once really existed but has now been lost, and its name, "Androgynous," meaning man-woman, survives only as an insult. Second, the original human beings, of all three kinds, were round, their backs and sides forming a circle. Each of them had four hands and four feet, and one head on a round neck, with two faces, exactly alike, looking in opposite directions. Each also had four ears, two sets of genitals, and everything else to match.
paragraphs.notes: Aristophanes' speech runs 5.0-5.7, so per the glossary each paragraph opens a single quote and only 5.7 closes it. 'The primeval man' made explicitly plural ('the original human beings, of all three kinds') so 5.1 can continue with 'they'. 'Androgynous' kept capitalized as Jowett has it, in nested double quotes, glossed as man-woman.

paragraphs.modern: 'They could walk upright, as people do now, backwards or forwards as they pleased. But they could also roll over and over at great speed, turning on their four hands and four feet, eight limbs in all, like acrobats turning cartwheels, going over and over with their legs in the air; that was how they ran when they wanted to go fast. There were three sexes, of the kinds I have described, because the sun, the moon, and the earth are three. The man was originally the child of the sun, the woman the child of the earth, and the man-woman the child of the moon, which is made up of sun and earth; and they were all round, and moved round and round, like their parents. Their strength and might were terrifying, their pride and ambition were enormous, and they launched an attack on the gods. They are the ones in the story of Otys and Ephialtes, the giant brothers who, as Homer says, dared to climb up to heaven and would have laid hands on the gods. The gods met in council in heaven and could not decide what to do. If they killed them and wiped out the whole race with thunderbolts, as they had once done to the giants, there would be an end of the sacrifices and worship that humans offered them. But on the other hand, the gods could not let such arrogance go unchecked. At last, after a great deal of thought, Zeus found a way. He said: "I think I have a plan that will humble their pride and improve their manners. Humans will go on existing, but I will cut each of them in two. Then they will be weaker in strength and greater in number, which will also have the advantage of making them more profitable to us.
paragraphs.notes: Zeus's speech is nested inside Aristophanes' speech, so it takes double quotes; it continues into 5.2, so neither quote closes here. 'Tumblers' rendered as acrobats turning cartwheels. The 'because' in the sun/moon/earth sentence is kept as Jowett's causal step.

paragraphs.modern: '"They will walk upright on two legs. And if they are still arrogant and will not keep quiet, I will split them again, and they can hop about on one leg." With that, he cut the humans in two, the way a sorb-apple, a small fruit, is halved for pickling, or the way you might slice an egg with a hair. As he cut them, one after another, he told Apollo to twist each one's face and half its neck around toward the cut side, so that the person could look at where he had been cut and learn a lesson in humility. Apollo was also told to heal their wounds and reshape their bodies. So Apollo turned the face around, and pulled the skin in from the sides over what we call the belly, gathering it like a drawstring purse. He made a single opening in the middle and tied it off in a knot, the one we call the navel. He also shaped the chest and smoothed out most of the wrinkles, much as a shoemaker smooths leather over a last, the foot-shaped block he works on. But he left a few wrinkles around the belly and navel, as a reminder of our original state. Once they had been cut in two, each half longed for its other half, and the halves came together. They threw their arms around one another, entwined in each other's embrace, longing to grow back into one; and they were on the point of dying of hunger and self-neglect, because they did not want to do anything apart. And when one half died and the other survived, the survivor looked for another mate — a man or a woman, as we call them now, though each was really only half of a whole man or a whole woman — and clung to that one.
paragraphs.notes: Opens with both marks: the single quote continues Aristophanes' speech and the double quote continues Zeus's, which closes after 'one leg.' Each simile glossed in a few words (sorb-apple, drawstring purse, shoemaker's last). 'Mouth' rendered as 'opening'; 'compose their forms' as 'reshape their bodies'.

paragraphs.modern: 'They were dying out when Zeus took pity on them and came up with a new plan. He moved their genitals round to the front, where they had not always been. Until then they had sown their seed not in one another but in the ground, the way grasshoppers lay their eggs in the earth; from then on they sowed it in one another. After this change, the male reproduced in the female, so that when a man and a woman embraced they would have children, and the race would continue; or, if a man came together with a man, they would be satisfied, and could rest, and get on with the business of life. That is how ancient our inborn desire for one another is. It brings our original nature back together, making one out of two and healing the human condition. Each of us, once separated and left with only one side, like a flatfish, is only half of a human being, like one half of a token split in two that matches nothing but its partner; and each of us is always looking for his other half. Men who are halves of the double being once called Androgynous are lovers of women; most adulterers come from this stock, and so do adulterous women who lust after men. Women who are halves of an original woman do not care for men, but are drawn to women; women who take other women as lovers are of this kind. But those who are halves of an original male pursue males. While they are young, being slices of the original man, they hang around men and embrace them; and they are the best of boys and young men, because they have the most manly nature.
paragraphs.notes: 'Indenture' rendered as its meaning, one half of a split token that matches only its partner (the same image as the tallies in 5.6). 'The female companions' made explicit as women who take other women as lovers. Frank, plain terms for genitals and reproduction.

paragraphs.modern: 'Some people say that they are shameless, but that is not true. They do not behave this way from any lack of shame, but because they are brave and manly and have a manly look, and they embrace what is like themselves. And when they grow up, these are the men who become our statesmen, and they are the only ones who do, which is strong proof that what I am saying is true. As grown men they are lovers of youths — that is, they court younger men — and by nature they are not inclined to marry or have children. If they do so at all, it is only because the law requires it; they are content to live with one another unmarried, if they are allowed to. A man of this nature is quick to love and ready to return love, always embracing what is akin to him. And when one of them meets his other half, the actual half of himself, whether he is a lover of youths or a lover of some other kind, the pair are lost in amazement, overcome by love and friendship and intimacy, and neither will let the other out of his sight even for a moment, so to speak. These are the people who spend their whole lives together, and yet they could not explain what they want from each other. For the intense longing each feels for the other does not seem to be a desire for sexual union, but for something else. The soul of each clearly desires something it cannot put into words, something it senses only darkly and doubtfully.
paragraphs.notes: 'Lovers of youth' glossed as courting younger men (the older lover courting the younger beloved). 'Lover's intercourse' rendered as sexual union. The last sentence is split so the soul's wordless, dimly sensed longing stands as a clear sentence of its own.

paragraphs.modern: 'Suppose Hephaestus, the blacksmith god, came with his tools to the pair as they lay side by side, and asked them, "What is it you people want from each other?" They would not be able to explain. And suppose further that, seeing how puzzled they were, he said: "Do you want to be wholly one, always together, day and night? Because if that is what you want, I am ready to melt you into one and let you grow together, so that the two of you will become one. As long as you live, you will share a single life, as if you were one person; and after you die, down in the world below, you will still be one departed soul instead of two. So I ask you: is this what your love desires, and would you be satisfied to have it?" Every one of them, on hearing this offer, would agree, and not one would deny, that this meeting and melting into one another, this becoming one instead of two, was the very expression of his age-old need. And the reason is that human nature was originally one and we were a whole, and the desire and pursuit of the whole is called love. There was a time, I say, when we were one; but now, because of the wickedness of humankind, the god has dispersed us, just as the Lacedaemonians, the Spartans, broke up the city of the Arcadians and dispersed its people into villages.
paragraphs.notes: Hephaestus's words are nested speech, so double quotes. The double negative is turned into 'every one would agree, and not one would deny'. Jowett's 'God' rendered 'the god' (Plato's ho theos), since a capital-G God reads as monotheistic today; Jowett's bracketed 'compare Arist. Pol.' notes omitted.

paragraphs.modern: 'And if we do not obey the gods, there is a danger that we will be split in two again and go about like the flat figures carved in profile on monuments, with only half a nose; and that we will be like tallies, those tokens split in two whose halves match only each other. So let us urge everyone to show reverence toward the gods, in order that we may avoid evil and obtain the good, which Love rules over and brings to us. And let no one oppose Love: whoever opposes him is an enemy of the gods. For if we are friends of the god and at peace with him, we will find the loves that are truly our own, which rarely happens in this world at present. I am being serious, so I must beg Eryximachus not to make fun of this, or to find in what I am saying any allusion to Pausanias and Agathon, who, I suspect, are both of the manly kind and belong to the class I have been describing. But my words apply more widely: they include men and women everywhere. And I believe that if our loves were perfectly fulfilled, and each of us, returning to his original nature, won his own original true love, then our race would be happy. And if that would be best of all, then the next best thing, as things are now, must be whatever comes nearest to that union: finding a love whose nature is truly akin to our own.
paragraphs.notes: 'Basso-relievo' rendered as flat figures carved in profile (low relief); tallies glossed as split tokens. 'Lord and minister' rendered as 'rules over and brings to us'. 'Congenial love' made explicit as a love whose nature is truly akin to ours (echoing 'akin' in 5.4). The wink about Pausanias and Agathon kept as Jowett's relative clause.

paragraphs.modern: 'So if we want to praise the one who has done us this good, we must praise the god Love, our greatest benefactor. In this life he leads us back to our own nature, and he gives us high hopes for the future, for he promises that if we are reverent toward the gods, he will restore us to our original state, and heal us, and make us happy and blessed. This, Eryximachus, is my speech about love. It is different from yours, but I must beg you not to make it a target for your jokes, so that each of the others may have his turn — each, or rather either, since Agathon and Socrates are the only ones left.'
paragraphs.notes: Light repair. 'Pious' rendered 'reverent toward the gods' to match 'reverence' in 5.6. The single quote closes here, at the end of Aristophanes' speech.

paragraphs.modern: Socrates said: 'You played your part well, Eryximachus. But if you were in my position now, or rather in the position I will be in once Agathon has spoken, you would indeed be completely at a loss.'
paragraphs.notes: 'In a great strait' rendered 'completely at a loss'. 'At a loss' is used for every recurrence of 'strait' (6.7, 6.8, 6.9).

paragraphs.modern: 'No,' replied Socrates, 'I would be very wrong to accuse you, Agathon, of that or any other lack of taste. And I am well aware that if you met people you thought wise, you would care much more about their opinion than about the opinion of the many. But then we cannot be counted among the select few who are wise, since we were part of the foolish many in the theatre. Still, I know that if you happened to find yourself in the presence, not of one of us, but of someone truly wise, you would be ashamed to disgrace yourself in front of him — wouldn't you?'
paragraphs.notes: Light repair; the trap question is kept as a tag question so 5.14 ('Yes') still answers it. 'Theatre' kept to match the KEEP neighbours 5.11 and 5.12 (American 'theater' would break the scene's consistency).

paragraphs.modern: Here Phaedrus interrupted them, saying: 'Do not answer him, my dear Agathon; for if he can only get a partner to talk with, especially a good-looking one, he will no longer care about finishing our plan. Now, I love to hear him talk; but just at present I must not forget the speech in praise of Love which I ought to receive from him and from everyone. When you and he have paid your tribute to the god, then you may talk.'
paragraphs.notes: Light repair. 'Encomium' replaced by 'speech in praise of Love', matching the proposal in 1.46 ('a speech in honor of Love') and R4's planned rendering of 'encomium' in chapter 7. Jowett's source drops 'Do' ('not answer him'); restored as in the current modern.

paragraphs.modern: The speakers before me, instead of praising the god Love or revealing his nature, seem to have congratulated mankind on the benefits he bestows on them. But I would rather praise the god first, and then speak of his gifts; that is always the right way to praise anything. May I say, without irreverence or offense, that of all the blessed gods Love is the most blessed, because he is the most beautiful and the best? And he is the most beautiful, first of all because he is the youngest. He himself is the witness of his own youth, for he flees from Old Age — and Old Age is swift enough, swifter, truly, than most of us would like. Love hates Old Age and will not come near him; but youth and love live and move together, for, as the proverb says, like is drawn to like. Phaedrus said many things about Love that I agree with; but I cannot agree that Love is older than Iapetus and Kronos, the ancient Titans. Not so! I maintain that he is the youngest of the gods, and forever young. The ancient doings among the gods, those deeds of divine violence that Hesiod and Parmenides told of, were, if the stories are true, the work of Necessity and not of Love. Had Love been there in those days, there would have been no chaining or mutilating of gods, and no other violence, but peace and sweetness, as there is now in heaven, ever since Love began to reign. Love is young, and he is also tender. He deserves a poet like Homer to describe his tenderness, the way Homer says of Ate, the goddess of ruin, that she is a goddess and tender:
paragraphs.notes: Agathon's speech (6.0-6.6) is left without enclosing quote marks to match the KEEP paragraphs 5.17 (which closes the quote before the speech), 6.1 and 6.5 (verse in single quotes) and 6.6 (the end of the speech, unquoted). Opening quotes here would leave the speech unclosed, since 6.6 cannot change. Age is named and capitalized as Old Age so 'him' is unambiguous. The paragraph still ends on the colon that leads into Homer's line in 6.1.

paragraphs.modern: Here is excellent proof of her tenderness: she walks not on what is hard, but on what is soft. Let me offer a similar proof of the tenderness of Love. He walks not on the earth, nor even on the skulls of men, which are not so very soft, but in the hearts and souls of both gods and men, which are the softest things of all: in them he walks and dwells and makes his home. Yet not in every soul without exception; for where there is hardness he departs, and where there is softness, there he dwells. And since he always nestles, with his feet and in every other way, in the softest of soft places, how can he be anything but the softest of all things? Truly, then, he is the tenderest as well as the youngest; and he is also supple in form. For if he were hard and unbending, he could not wrap himself around all things, or wind his way unnoticed into and out of every human soul. And proof of his suppleness and the fine proportions of his form is his grace, which everyone agrees belongs to Love in a special way; gracelessness and love are forever at war with each other. The beauty of his coloring is shown by his home among the flowers. For he does not live among beauties that have no bloom or are fading, whether of body or soul or anything else; but wherever there are flowers and scents, there he settles, and there he stays. About the beauty of the god I have said enough — and yet there is much more that I could say.
paragraphs.notes: Begins as a new sentence after Homer's verse in 6.1. 'Flexile/flexure' rendered supple/unbending; 'ungrace' rendered gracelessness; 'fairness of his complexion' rendered 'the beauty of his coloring', not pale skin. Agathon's balanced antitheses (hardness/softness, settles/stays) kept.

paragraphs.modern: Now I must speak of his virtue. His greatest glory is that he neither does wrong to any god or any man, nor suffers wrong from any god or any man. The reason is that if anything is done to him, it is not done by force, since force never comes near him; and when he acts, he does not act by force. For everyone serves Love in everything of their own free will, and where there is willing agreement, there, as the laws that are the lords of the city declare, is justice. So he is just; and not only just, but supremely self-controlled. For self-control is acknowledged to be the ruler of the pleasures and desires, and no pleasure ever masters Love: he is their master, and they are his servants. And if he conquers them, he must be self-controlled indeed. As for courage, even Ares, the God of War, is no match for him. Ares is the captive and Love is the lord; for love, his love for Aphrodite, masters him, as the story goes; and the master is stronger than the servant. And if Love conquers the bravest of all the others, he himself must be the bravest. I have spoken of his courage and justice and self-control; but I have yet to speak of his wisdom, and I must try to do my best, as far as my ability allows. In the first place, he is a poet — and here, like Eryximachus, I am praising my own art — and he is also the source of poetry in others, which he could not be if he were not a poet himself.
paragraphs.notes: 'Temperate/Temperance' rendered self-controlled/self-control (glossary). Ares named as the God of War. Connectives made explicit ('The reason is that', 'So he is just') without strengthening Agathon's argument. Jowett's parenthesis rendered with dashes.

paragraphs.modern: At his touch, everyone becomes a poet, even one who had no music in him before; and this too is proof that Love is a good poet, accomplished in all the fine arts, for no one can give another what he does not have himself, or teach what he does not know. Who will deny that the creation of the animals is his doing? Are they not all works of his wisdom, conceived and born through him? And as for the artists, do we not know that only the one whom Love inspires comes into the light of fame, while the one whom Love never touches remains in obscurity? Apollo discovered the arts of medicine and archery and divination under the guidance of love and desire, so he too is a disciple of Love. So too the melody of the Muses, the metalwork of Hephaestus, the weaving of Athene, and the rule of Zeus over gods and men are all owed to Love, who invented them. And so Love set the realm of the gods in order — the love of beauty, clearly, for Love has nothing to do with ugliness. In the old days, as I said at the start, dreadful deeds were done among the gods, because they were ruled by Necessity; but ever since Love was born, every good thing in heaven and on earth has sprung from the Love of the beautiful. Therefore, Phaedrus, I say of Love that he is himself the most beautiful and the best, and the cause of all that is most beautiful and best in everything else. And a line of poetry comes into my mind in which he is said to be the god who
paragraphs.notes: Jowett's bracketed note on the Euripides fragment omitted, as in the current modern. 'Deformity' rendered ugliness; 'fairest' rendered most beautiful. Ends on 'the god who' so the verse in 6.5 still completes the sentence.

paragraphs.modern: When Agathon had finished speaking, Aristodemus said that everyone cheered; the young man was thought to have spoken in a way worthy of himself and of the god. And Socrates, looking at Eryximachus, said: 'Tell me, son of Acumenus, was I not right to be afraid? And was I not a true prophet when I said that Agathon would make a wonderful speech, and that I would be at a loss?'
paragraphs.notes: Light repair; 'in a strait' rendered 'at a loss', as in 5.9, 6.8 and 6.9.

paragraphs.modern: 'The part of the prophecy about Agathon,' replied Eryximachus, 'seems to me to be true; but not the other part — that you will be at a loss.'
paragraphs.notes: Light repair; same 'at a loss' as 5.9, 6.7 and 6.9.

paragraphs.modern: 'Why, my dear friend,' said Socrates, 'wouldn't I, or anyone, be at a loss, having to speak after hearing such a rich and varied speech? I am especially struck by the beauty of the closing words — who could listen to them without amazement? When I thought how immeasurably inferior my own powers are, I was ready to run away in shame, if there had been any way to escape. For the speech reminded me of Gorgias, the famous orator; and at its end I imagined Agathon shaking at me the Gorginian — or should I say Gorgonian — head of that great master of rhetoric. Like the head of the monster Gorgon, it was meant simply to turn me and my speech to stone, as Homer says, and strike me dumb. And then I realized how foolish I had been to agree to take my turn with you in praising love, and to say that I too was a master of the art, when in fact I had no idea how anything ought to be praised. For in my simplicity I imagined that whatever is said in praise should be true; and that, with truth as the starting point, the speaker should choose the finest of these truths and set them out in the best way. And I felt quite proud, thinking that I knew the nature of true praise and would speak well. But now I see that the idea was to credit Love with every kind of greatness and glory, whether it really belonged to him or not, without regard to truth or falsehood — that did not matter. For the original proposal, it seems, was not that each of you should really praise Love, but only that you should appear to praise him.
paragraphs.notes: Socrates' speech runs 6.9-6.10: the quote opens here and closes only at the end of 6.10. The Gorgias/Gorgon pun is kept with both of Jowett's adjectives, and Gorgias (the orator) and the Gorgon (the monster whose head turns people to stone) are each identified in a few words. Jowett's '(Odyssey)' note omitted. His view of praise is laid out in order: tell the truth, choose the finest truths, present them well.

paragraphs.modern: 'And so you attribute to Love every imaginable form of praise that can be gathered from anywhere; and you say that "he is all this," and "the cause of all that," making him appear the most beautiful and best of all to people who do not know him — for you cannot fool those who do. And what a noble, solemn hymn of praise you have delivered! But since I misunderstood the nature of the praise when I said that I would take my turn, I must beg to be released from the promise I made in ignorance, which, as Euripides would say, was a promise of the lips and not of the mind. So goodbye to that style of praise, for I do not praise in that way — no, indeed, I cannot. But if you would like to hear the truth about love, I am ready to speak in my own manner, though I will not make myself ridiculous by entering into any rivalry with you. So tell me, Phaedrus, whether you would like to hear the truth about love, spoken in whatever words and in whatever order happen to come into my mind at the time. Would that suit you?'
paragraphs.notes: Light repair. Opening single quote added (continuation of Socrates' speech from 6.9); nested quotations in double quotes as in the current modern. Jowett's '(Eurip. Hyppolytus)' note omitted.
